title: Who is like you? (Exodus 15:11)
hookLine: the Song of the Sea returns: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?"
last: MORE THAN A DOZEN WORDS, ALL SAYING YES.

cards: Twelve days ago, the Song of the Sea closed the verses of song. Since then: Barchu, the light, the angels, great love, the Shema and its three paragraphs, and the word true. You might think the sea was left behind.
It isn't. As the blessing after the Shema builds, it tells the story of the rescue again, then quotes one line from that song, and in many synagogues everyone sings it together.

teach.h: WHO IS LIKE UNTO THEE, O LORD?
teach.b: The line is from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty? Who is like unto Thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?"
In Hebrew it begins mi chamocha, who is like you. The blessing sets it up as a scene: Moses and the people of Israel sang to you with great joy, and all of them said, mi chamocha.
A little later it says the rescued sang a new song at the shore, and quotes the song's last line too: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever."
It's a question, but nobody's waiting for an answer. It's the kind you ask when you're amazed: who does that?
The word translated mighty, elim, can also mean gods, and in the song's own world each nation had its gods; the song says none of them did what was done at the sea. There's a harder reading, too.

teach.h: AMONG THE SILENT: A HARDER READING.
teach.b: A teaching in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, adds one letter and reads among the silent: who is like you, who sees suffering and keeps silent?
It sits in the Talmud's account of the Temple's destruction, a reading born of grief. Both readings live in the tradition.
And a later tradition says the Maccabees' name comes from the first letters of mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai. Others connect the name to a word for hammer, and the question is still debated.
Every morning, though, the line is sung as it began: a question of wonder, from people standing on the far shore.

how: Mi Chamocha is part of the blessing after the Shema in the morning and evening services; in many synagogues the congregation sings it together, and the blessing then leads toward the standing prayer.

games.q: the Temple has been destroyed. a teacher reads Mi Chamocha and can't say among the mighty. what does the Talmud record?
o: the line is dropped from prayer.
it's read as among the silent: who sees suffering and keeps silent?
the teacher refuses to read it at all.
games.why: the school of Rabbi Ishmael read elim as illmim, the silent. the line stayed in the prayer book; the harder reading stayed in the tradition.

practice: Think of something that amazed you lately, a kindness you didn't expect, a sunset, a child's sentence, and instead of describing it, ask it the way the song does: who does that? Let the question sit without an answer.
If you pray, you can say mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai.
